mcqs.question: `Square extends Rectangle` and overrides `setWidth` to also adjust height, keeping the shape square. Structurally it has every Rectangle method with matching signatures. Does it satisfy the Liskov Substitution Principle?
options: Yes — having the same method signatures as the parent class is sufficient for Liskov substitution
No — Liskov substitution is behavioral, and Square breaks Rectangle's implicit contract that setWidth changes width only, even though the method signatures match exactly
Yes, as long as Square is a subclass keyword-wise, regardless of what its methods actually do
No, because Square and Rectangle cannot share any method names at all
mcqs.explanation: Liskov substitution requires that provable properties of the supertype still hold for the subtype in practice, not just matching method signatures — Square's setWidth side-effect on height violates a caller's reasonable expectation despite identical signatures. Matching signatures alone is exactly the insufficient structural check this Subtopic warns about, and the two classes obviously do share method names.

mcqs.question: Given `Dog <: Animal`, under what variance relationship does `Container<Animal> <: Container<Dog>` hold (the relationship flipped from the element relationship)?
options: Covariance
Contravariance — this flip is safe specifically for containers that only consume the type parameter, like a function parameter
Invariance
This relationship can never hold under any variance rule
mcqs.explanation: A flipped subtyping direction relative to the element type is exactly what contravariance means, and it's sound for purely-consuming positions — a handler for any Animal can safely substitute for one needing only Dogs. Covariance preserves direction rather than flipping it, invariance has no relationship at all, and this flipped relationship is a real, named, and useful case, not an impossibility.

mcqs.question: `Animal[] animals = new Dog[3]; animals[0] = new Cat();` compiles in Java. What actually happens when this code runs?
options: It runs successfully and stores the Cat in the array with no issue
It throws ArrayStoreException at runtime, because Java arrays remember their actual element type and check every write against it, even though the static type animals[0] = ... satisfied the compiler
It fails to compile after all, contradicting the premise
It silently converts the Cat into a Dog to satisfy the array's real element type
mcqs.explanation: Java's array covariance is unsafe specifically because the compiler only checks the static Animal[] type, while the array's actual runtime element type (Dog[]) is checked separately on every write, throwing ArrayStoreException when they disagree — exactly the trap this Subtopic describes. It does not run successfully, does compile as stated, and there is no silent type conversion happening.

mcqs.question: Why is `(Animal) -> Dog` a subtype of `(Dog) -> Animal`, rather than the seemingly more intuitive `(Dog) -> Animal` being a subtype of `(Animal) -> Dog`?
options: Because return types are covariant (Dog satisfies a need for at least Animal) and parameter types are contravariant (accepting any Animal satisfies a need to accept Dog specifically) — both directions checked independently give this exact relationship
Because function types have no variance rules at all and the relationship is arbitrary
Because Dog and Animal are unrelated when used as function types, regardless of their class relationship
Because parameter types are covariant and return types are contravariant, the reverse of the stated rule
mcqs.explanation: Checking each half of the signature against substitutability separately — parameters contravariant, returns covariant — is exactly what produces this specific, correctly-derived relationship, not an arbitrary or reversed rule. Function types absolutely have well-defined variance, and the class relationship between Dog and Animal is precisely what's being used to derive it.

mcqs.question: Why can't a mutable generic collection like `MutableList<T>` be safely covariant, even though `Dog <: Animal`?
options: If MutableList<Dog> could substitute for MutableList<Animal>, code holding the Animal-typed reference could legally call add(Cat()), inserting a Cat into what is actually a Dog-only list underneath
Mutable collections cannot hold reference types at all, only primitives
Covariance is a purely theoretical concept with no relevance to mutable containers
MutableList<T> is always contravariant instead, never covariant or invariant
mcqs.explanation: The exact hole covariance opens for a mutable, writable container is that the supertype-typed reference can add elements the underlying subtype-typed collection shouldn't accept, corrupting it — which is why invariance is required once both read and write are possible. Mutable collections hold reference types constantly, covariance is a very real practical concern here, and MutableList<T> is invariant by default, not contravariant.

mcqs.question: Why does Java use use-site variance (wildcards like `? extends Animal`) instead of declaration-site variance (like Kotlin's `out T`)?
options: Java's generics were added after the language already existed, onto a large ecosystem of already-invariant classes, so a mechanism that grants variance without changing existing class declarations was the realistic retrofit path
Use-site variance is strictly more powerful and declaration-site variance cannot express contravariance at all
Java classes are physically incapable of declaring variance in their syntax
Wildcards were added purely for symmetry with C++ templates, with no relation to Java's own generics history
mcqs.explanation: The historical retrofit constraint — adding variance without rewriting already-existing invariant class declarations — is exactly why Java chose use-site wildcards; Kotlin, designed with variance from the start, could commit to declaration-site cleanly. Declaration-site variance handles contravariance just fine (Kotlin's `in T`), Java's syntax could in principle support declaration-site annotations, and this has nothing to do with C++ templates.
